newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia pledges to help settle garment strikes.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia pledges to help settle garment strikes.

text.p: The Cambodian government pledged on Tuesday to help resolve the latest labour dispute to hit the country's garment sector after scores of strikers marched in protest to the Industry Ministry.

Nearly 200 workers of the Malaysian-owned Supreme Garments Pte Ltd marched through central Phnom Penh after striking earlier in the day to press for better working conditions, more pay and shorter hours.

It was the sixth industrial dispute to hit the garment sector in the past month. Four companies have agreed new terms with their workers, while Hong Kong-owned Tack Fat Co is still in dispute with its striking staff.

Industry Minister Pou Sothirak met 10 worker representatives from Supreme Garments and told them and reporters that he would go to their factory on Wednesday to witness elections of seven representatives to negotiate grievances with the factory owners.
Pou Sothirak said his ministry would also act as a mediator between the two sides, while adding that the strike should be resolved internally and not be complicated by politics.

"I appeal (to) some politicians, please withdraw your influence from this so as not to turn it into a political affair," he said in a clear reference to opposition leader Sam Rainsy, who has led the recent strikes.
He said he sympathised with the workers' protests but that in future they should first convey their grievances to the ministry.
A Supreme Garments spokeswoman said the workers had not made any requests from management or announced any strike action.
"We will just let them strike," she said. "What can we do? What can I do? ...We just want them to tell us what they want."
Sam Rainsy waited outside the Industry Ministry with striking workers as six fire engines arrived to disperse the marchers who eventually went home peacefully.
The Khmer Nation Party president said the strikes and a dozen protests had produced results and improved conditions in some factories.
He welcomed plans by First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh to convene a meeting of garment owners, members of parliament, government officials and possibly workers.
"I think that Prince Ranariddh has come up with a good formula to try to unblock the situation. He doesn't want to see these labour disputes going on and on," he said.
Cambodia's 38 garment factories, which turn out everything from overalls to denim hot pants, were until a month ago heralded as an economic success story for this war-scarred nation.

Analysts say that after several years of ignoring complaints from workers over poor working conditions, Cambodia has found its policy of investors first, labour second, has given birth to a modern labour movement -- with the garment sector as just its first target.
